name: キラメキノ青空 (Kirameki no Aozora)

claims.text: Standard ramen and mazesoba shop: bowls are built on wheat noodles with a wheat-based shoyu/tare element, so wheat is a core ingredient throughout the menu.
The kitchen is built around chicken broth and meat toppings (chicken chashu, minced meat in the mazesoba), so there is heavy meat contact across all preparations.

name: キラメキノトリ (Kirameki no Tori)

claims.text: The kitchen handles wheat ramen noodles, Taiwan mazesoba (wheat noodles) and wheat-dredged karaage, so heavy gluten cross-contact is unavoidable in this environment.
The chicken-paitan bowls are offered in shoyu and miso versions, whose tare uses standard wheat-containing soy sauce/miso; even the shio version is a wheat-noodle dish.
The broth is a chicken-bone paitan simmered with chicken meat and skin and topped with chicken chashu; there is no plant-based broth or noodle option, so no vegan service is possible.
Wheat-noodle tantanmen cooked in shared pots in a Chinese kitchen that also fries and wok-cooks; no gluten-free handling is described anywhere.
As a Cantonese restaurant and a tantanmen specialist, dishes rely on standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce and likely wheat-based tare; no wheat-free soy is mentioned.
Meat- and seafood-forward kitchen with a pork/sesame tantanmen base; no separated vegan prep is indicated.
As a full Chinese restaurant, dishes rely on standard (wheat-based) soy sauce and seasonings; no wheat-free tare or sauce is indicated.
The signature tantanmen is built on house-made pork meat-miso over a chicken-bone broth, so shared pots and broths make vegan separation impractical.

name: コムギノキラメキ 上桂前田町本店 (Komugi no Kirameki Kamikatsura Maedacho Hont)

claims.text: Self-described as a wheat-noodle shop ('コムギ／小麦') with an on-site noodle factory, so wheat is central and pervasive throughout the kitchen; no gluten-free option exists.
The chicken-paitan ramen is offered in a soy-sauce (醤油) variety; standard ramen shoyu tare is typically wheat-based, and no wheat-free seasoning is indicated.
All signature bowls are animal-based — chicken broth, minced pork, egg yolk; no vegan items are prepared, so there is no separated vegan line.

name: コムギノキラメキ〈小麦〉 (Komugi no Kirameki (Komugi))

claims.text: House noodles are wheat (a four-wheat blend), milled and made in-house, and used across every bowl; there is no gluten-free noodle and no allergen-handling program advertised, so cross-contamination from shared noodle water and prep is unavoidable.
Soy- and miso-tare ramen are on the menu; standard ramen tare and miso in Japan are wheat-containing, and no wheat-free tare is indicated.
Broth is chicken-paitan and dishes feature pork, egg yolk, and fish powder; no plant-based options were found, so vegan diners cannot eat here safely.

name: 昆布と麺 喜一 (Konbu to Men Kiichi)

claims.text: The dish is wheat-noodle ramen/tsukemen with no gluten-free alternative noted, so cross-contamination is moot for celiacs — the meal itself contains gluten.

The signature kombu ramen is stated to use no kaeshi / no soy-sauce tare (かえしは不使用), so the flagship broth avoids the usual wheat-shoyu seasoning; however, an account of the gagome kombu tsukemen describes a soy-sauce tare.
Broth relies on bonito and seafood (and at least one bowl uses pork chashu), so it is not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diners.
The signature kombu ramen broth uses no additives and no meat stock — a purely kombu-and-seafood dashi (添加物、肉類、かえしは不使用), unusually transparent and animal-stock-free for ramen.

name: こういうもん家 Ro-ji (Kouiumonya Ro-ji)

claims.text: Tantanmen uses wheat ramen noodles (Kushiro Seimen) boiled in shared water; no gluten-free handling is mentioned.
No source specifies the tare ingredients, but a sesame tantan tare of this style standardly uses wheat-based soy sauce; treat as containing wheat.
Broth is meat-based with ground pork topping; no vegan preparation described.
Kitchen will omit the finishing chili oil on request, so the bowl can be made milder.
